Before anyone explains how the Academy works, the intake printer gives one mechanical cough.
Then it prints nothing.
Instead, a black envelope slides from the tray.
No stamp.
No sender.
One strange mark: 0.
Inside is a blank Detective Academy Recruit Credential.
No name.
No call sign.
No detective assigned.
A mistake?
A coincidence?
OR AN INVITATION MEANT FOR YOU?
WILL YOU CLAIM IT?

The Detective Academy is where small real-world mysteries become case files.
New calls, reopened records, and strange pieces of evidence arrive through the Academy intake desk.
Take a look inside.
This is how it all begins.

WHAT TO EXPECT
01 CLUE INSPECTION
02 READING WITNESS STATEMENTS
03 COMPARING EVIDENCE
04 STUDYING MAPS & COORDINATES
05 DECODING MESSAGES
06 FOLLOWING PATTERNS
LOOK CLOSER. CHECK THE FACTS. LET THE EVIDENCE LEAD.
WHAT YOU ARE ABOUT TO WALK INTO
The Academy is not one room, and this investigation will not happen in one afternoon.

30 CONNECTED CASE FILES
Witness-board mysteries, map and coordinate puzzles, visual evidence, secret codes, timelines, sequencing challenges and logic deductions.

A TEAM THAT THINKS TOGETHER
The Happy Makers will be your team.
They compare clues, trade theories, drop case notes, make jokes at extremely professional moments and point out things worth checking.

YOU MAKE THE CALL
They do not get to make your verdict for you.
The maps grow larger, and different cases ask you to test the evidence in different ways.

STRANGER THINGS HAPPEN
A trophy returns before anyone logs it. A box marked EVIDENCE lands where it should not. Later, solved maps and forgotten records begin to matter again.

And somewhere inside the Academy, one question keeps returning:
WHAT IS ROOM ZERO?
LET'S MEET THE HAPPY MAKERS

MEET THE HAPPY MAKERS
THE ACADEMY FIELD TEAM

WHO THEY ARE
Five field detectives. One archive mentor.
Mimi, her children Luli, Dilo, Alio and Nini, and Grandma Bibi.
A family with six different ways of looking at the same mess.
They compare clues, challenge each other's theories and keep asking questions until the story starts to make sense.

HOW THEY WORK
Clues first.
Theories second.
Arguments occasionally.
Then they test what actually fits and quietly retire the theory that sounded brilliant five minutes ago.

WHY A TEAM?
Because no one notices everything.
Luckily, they rarely miss the same thing.
Bad news for mysteries.

HOW EVERY CASE WORKS
YOU NEVER NEED TO GUESS WHAT TO DO NEXT. EVERY CASE FOLLOWS THE SAME SIMPLE RHYTHM.

3 EVIDENCE

4 HAPPY MAKERS CHAT
The squad thinks out loud, jokes, questions theories and helps you notice what deserves attention.

Use the response made for that case: circle it, mark it, sort it, enter the code or write the coordinate. Then move on.

Only some cases send something to the Case Wall. When the book says “CASE WALL → PAGE 13”, copy that item there. Otherwise keep the verdict on the case page.

Some cases use an Academy floor grid to reconstruct where people were standing. Use these rules unless a case gives a more specific instruction.
1 COORDINATES
Letters label columns from left to right. Numbers label rows from top to bottom.
D3 = column D, row 3. Use the labels printed beside the map you are solving.
2 PLACE THE WITNESSES
Use only printed witness statements, the map key and visible map features.
1. Place every witness exactly once, on a usable square.
2. Each witness must use a different row and a different column.
3. Start with a certain position. Cross its row and column off the options for everyone else, then check the clues again.
4. “Exactly one other person” means two people in that named room or area in total. Use this clue while placing people, not just after you finish.
5. A room companion is a lead for the next interview, not automatically guilty.
6. Keep every final position on the completed map. Do not erase it after recording the verdict.
3 CLUE WORDS
BESIDE: one square up, down, left or right, in the same room or area. Diagonals and squares across a wall do not count.
DIAGONALLY NEXT TO: exactly one row and one column away; the two squares touch at a corner.
NORTH / SOUTH / EAST / WEST: up / down / right / left. North-west means above and left; the two distances need not match. The same applies to the other paired directions.
A row-distance clue fixes only the row difference; a column-distance clue fixes only the column difference, unless the clue also specifies the other direction.
GRID STEPS: add the row difference and the column difference. Count grid distance, not a walking route around walls.
OUTER WALL: the outside edge of the whole grid.
4 READ EACH CASE'S MAP KEY
A printed open circle means an object square is usable. A printed black square means it is blocked. Follow the marker when an object has one.
Otherwise, use clear floor and only the objects permitted by that case's key. Other object squares are blocked.
Use named room or area boundaries when checking who shares a space. Case 26 gives its own room-and-zone key for the later map task.
